courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Alpha compositing sorted splats at one pixel
md: Pixel color is a weighted sum of splat colors with weights $\alpha_i T_i$. Order changes who gets the weight, and every splat with nonzero weight receives a gradient.

courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: Hazard pointers and epochs: stop reuse while anyone looks
md: Choose by failure mode. Tagged pointers: cheap, but need wide CAS or spare bits and type-stable nodes. LL/SC: ABA-free in principle, rarely usable directly. Hazard pointers: bounded garbage under stalls, cost per access. Epochs: cheapest per access, but one stalled thread blocks all reclamation.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Who are you, and what may you do: authentication vs authorization
md: Being logged in is not a permission. Authentication tells the server *who* is asking; it says nothing about *which* objects and functions that person may touch. Each request needs both answers.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Cases: USPS, Peloton and Optus, APIs that trusted too much
md: Adding a login in front of an endpoint is not the fix for broken authorization. Peloton's partial fix and USPS's whole design show the result: every registered user, and anyone can register, gets everyone's data.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: NTLM relay: forwarding someone else's login, and how signing stops it
md: Relay borrows a live NTLM sign-in instead of stealing a hash. It is stopped by binding authentication to the session or channel: SMB signing, LDAP signing and channel binding, and EPA on HTTPS. Then remove the bait: LLMNR, NBT-NS and NTLM itself. To respond, isolate the rogue host, review what the relayed identity did on the target, and revoke any certificate issued through a relayed login.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: DCSync: asking a domain controller for every password
md: DCSync abuses a legitimate protocol: anyone with both replication rights can ask a DC for any password hash. Control who holds those rights, audit 4662 with the replication GUIDs, and treat a DCSync as compromise of every account.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Why documents and scripts: the chain an analyst unpicks
md: Every demo in this course uses harmless files built for it. Never fetch real samples onto a work machine: get them only through your organisation's incident process, keep them zipped with a password, and open them only in the isolated lab described in the malware course.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Unpacking II: dumping from memory, and payloads hidden in data
md: Carve, decode, confirm. Find where the code reads data, extract exactly those bytes, decode them step by step, and check each step against the code that does it. A decoding you guessed is a hypothesis until the code agrees.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: Return-oriented programming as Shacham defined it
md: Misconception: "ROP needs special gadget functions, so removing dangerous library functions stops it." Shacham's thesis is the opposite: any large enough body of x86 code contains enough sequences, many of them unintended. The fix is checking control flow, not pruning code.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Command and control at the design level
md: Do not treat C2 detection as "find the red team's tool". CISA's federal red team (AA24-193A) "deployed over seven different implants" with different host and network signatures precisely to show that defenders who hunt one framework's fingerprints miss the rest. Detect the behaviour every implant shares: periodic contact, new destinations, odd egress from servers.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Reporting, retesting and where to practise
md: Measure a red or purple team by what it changes: findings with owners, fixes retested with the same procedure, and tests that keep running afterwards. Everything is done under written authorisation, inside agreed rules, with a way to stop in minutes.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: From one model call to an agent loop
md: The model does not execute tools. It only emits a structured request. Whether a shell command actually runs, and with what permissions, is decided entirely by harness code, which is why safety controls belong in the harness.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: The read path: scoring memories by recency, importance and relevance
md: Recency decay does not resolve conflicts. A stale fact with high importance and relevance still makes the cut, so the newer fact helps only if the reader happens to trust it more. Resolve contradictions on the write path; use scoring to choose among facts that are all still true.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: From a benchmark to an environment: reset, step and a checker
md: An agentic RL environment is a benchmark task turned into a loop you can run millions of times: `reset` to a clean sandbox, `step` per tool call, and a programmatic checker that produces the reward at the end. The simulated user in tau-bench is part of the environment, not part of the policy.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: A toy agent loop: watching a web page give orders
md: The dangerous line is never the model call. It is the loop that turns model output into actions. Put your controls there.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Model supply chain: pickle files, safetensors and signing
md: Loading a pickle is running code. Prefer safetensors, load PyTorch files with weights_only=True, and verify a signature or hash from a source you trust before loading anything.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: Cheap surrogates for DFT: graph networks and interatomic potentials
md: Judge a discovery surrogate by what it does to DFT spending: precision (hit rate), recall, and DAF on unrelaxed inputs. A low regression error does not guarantee good decisions near the hull.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Build it yourself: a green-list watermark and detector in 60 lines
md: The two p-values for the watermarked run differ by a factor of about 78,000 ($5.9 \times 10^{-30}$ versus $4.6 \times 10^{-25}$). Both are tiny here, but the same gap at a borderline score decides whether someone is accused. Three Bricks reports exact tests because the normal tail is too optimistic exactly where thresholds sit, deep in the tail.

courseTitle: Allocation tracing and replay
lessonTitle: Capturing calls: glibc mtrace and LD_PRELOAD interposers
md: What interposition misses: statically linked programs (LD_PRELOAD is a feature of the dynamic linker), secure-execution binaries such as set-user-ID programs (the linker ignores LD_PRELOAD paths with slashes), and any memory that bypasses malloc: direct mmap, custom arenas and pools, GPU allocations. heaptrack's README notes pool allocators need code annotations to be profiled.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Local Outlier Factor: density compared with your neighbors
md: LOF answers a different question from Isolation Forest: not how isolated a point is, but how isolated it is relative to its own neighborhood. Use it when normal data has regions of very different density; pay for it with k-nearest-neighbor searches and a k to tune.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: The OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023), item by item
md: Most of the API Top 10 is not exotic. It is a missing check (who owns this, who may call this, how many times), a forgotten endpoint, or misplaced trust in another system.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: OpenID Connect: logging users in with an ID token
md: ID token: for the client, proves a login happened (check aud = your client_id and nonce). Access token: for the API, grants access (the API checks aud = itself). Never accept one where the other is expected.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Detecting and responding to API and token attacks
md: Tokens move the security perimeter into data: who issued it, with which key, for which audience, for how long. Log those fields on every request, alert on the impossible ones, and rehearse revoking at scale.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Writing rules: Semgrep and CodeQL on the same code
md: Write a custom rule when a bug teaches you a pattern: after every incident or review finding, ask "where else does this pattern appear?" and encode it. That is variant analysis, and it turns one fix into a class fix.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: SSVC: decisions instead of scores
md: SSVC turns "how bad is it?" into "what do we do, and how fast?". The inputs that matter most are exploitation status and your own context: exposure and how essential the system is. A score cannot know the second.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Restart part 2: undo, CLRs, and crashing during recovery
md: ARIES in one line: **repeat history, then undo the losers, logging every undo as a redo-only CLR whose UndoNextLSN skips what is already undone**. That makes recovery **idempotent**, meaning that running it again after a partial run ends in the same state as running it once: crash during analysis or redo and you simply start over; crash during undo and you resume where the CLRs say.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Why a plain loop is too slow and a plain gather is too fast
md: `gather` does not cancel siblings on failure. With the default `return_exceptions=False`, the first exception propagates to the caller but the docs state the other awaitables "won't be cancelled and will continue to run". If you want per-item errors without losing the batch, pass `return_exceptions=True` and inspect each result; if one failure should stop everything, use a `TaskGroup`.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Cooperative scheduling: blocking, budgets and cancellation
md: The budget only helps tasks that keep awaiting **Tokio** resources. It cannot interrupt a tight CPU loop or a blocking call, and the Tokio team has said it will not detect blocked workers and add threads automatically. Fixing those is your job.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: From a waveform to 0.96 s log-mel patches
md: A pretrained audio model never sees a whole clip at once. It sees fixed 0.96 s log-mel patches and returns one embedding and one score vector per patch. Everything about clip-level decisions (lesson 3) is about combining those per-patch outputs.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: How offline cracking works: guesses, lists, rules and arithmetic
md: Offline cracking = guess, hash, compare, at the attacker's full hardware speed. Defenders control two things: how many guesses a password needs (length, unpredictability, blocklists) and how expensive each guess is (a slow, salted hash).

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Wearing MFA down: SIM swaps, push fatigue and Uber 2022
md: MFA is only as strong as its weakest step. SMS inherits the phone network's weaknesses; plain push inherits human fatigue. Number matching helps against fatigue; phishing-resistant MFA removes the whole class.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: End-to-end science agents: AI Scientist and co-scientist
md: End-to-end science agents fail at the steps where nothing external checks them: invented numbers, unfair comparisons, edits to their own limits. Put independent checks (sandboxes, reproducibility, human experts) at exactly those points.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: x86-64 on Linux and macOS: the System V calling convention
md: Do not apply Windows habits to Linux binaries. On Windows the first argument is in `rcx`; on Linux and macOS `rcx` is the fourth. Misreading the convention shifts every argument by several positions and makes a correct analysis look nonsensical. Check the file format first: PE means Microsoft x64, ELF or Mach-O on x86-64 means System V.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Ternary weights: log2(3), absmean and the power of zero
md: "1-bit LLM" is the family name, not the bit count. BitNet b1.58 weights are ternary (about 1.58 bits), the original BitNet was binary (1 bit), and in both the activations are 8-bit and the embeddings stay in higher precision.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Build it yourself: train a tiny BitNet and run it from packed bytes
md: The whole method fits on a laptop: a quantizer in the forward pass, an STE in the backward pass, then 2 bits per weight and integer adds at inference. The hard part in practice is the kernel, and matching training's quantizers exactly.

courseTitle: Browser security internals: architecture, sandboxes and patch gaps
lessonTitle: A browser runs hostile code all day: the threat model
md: Misconception: "a sandbox escape is worse than a renderer bug, so it must be Critical." Chromium rates a renderer sandbox escape **High** because it needs the precondition of a compromised renderer. Critical is reserved for bugs that reach privileged code straight from a web page, or full chains.

courseTitle: Browser security internals: architecture, sandboxes and patch gaps
lessonTitle: Memory safety strategy: the Rule of 2, MiraclePtr, Rust and RLBox
md: Misconception: "a sandbox makes a memory bug harmless." It makes it worth less. A sandboxed decoder bug still gives code execution inside that sandbox, which is why Chromium still fixes and rewards such bugs as High, and why the Rule of 2 prefers removing the unsafe language when it can.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Compaction: merging sorted runs and organizing levels
md: Compaction converts a growing pile of overlapping files into a few large sorted runs. It is what keeps LSM reads and space bounded, and it is paid for with extra writes: every byte is rewritten each time it moves down a level.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: LRU-K: evict by the K-th most recent reference
md: LRU-K is not "keep the last K timestamps and you are done". Without a correlated reference period, a transaction that touches a page twice in a millisecond makes it look hot; without retained history, every page re-entering the pool starts at infinite distance and is evicted first.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Availability engineering: nines, redundancy and failure domains
md: Availability = uptime over total time. Hard dependencies multiply availabilities; independent redundant copies multiply failure rates; MTTR is a lever as strong as MTBF. Redundancy is only as good as its independence, so map failure domains, including software versions and admin identities.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Backups attackers cannot reach: immutability and isolated recovery
md: Assume production identity is lost. Give backups their own control plane, immutable and time-based retention, delayed and out-of-band-approved deletions, keys you cannot lose, alerts on every significant change, and restore into an isolated environment before anything returns to production.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Regulated resilience: DORA testing, TLPT and UK impact tolerances
md: DORA requires a BIA, backup and restore procedures with segregated restore systems, yearly continuity and switchover tests, a crisis function, and TLPT on production every three years for designated firms. The UK sets impact tolerances per important business service and requires proof, by severe but plausible scenario tests, that firms stay within them.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Generating with patches: the BLT decoding loop and its real cost
md: In BLT generation the latent model runs only when a patch closes, but the entropy model, encoder and decoder run on every byte in sequence. Fewer FLOPs per byte and lower latency are different goals; fixed patches, caches and speculative drafting are the levers for the second.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Data races: pthreads in C versus Send and Sync in Rust
md: Data race: unsynchronized conflicting accesses, undefined behavior, ruled out at compile time by the borrow rules plus Send and Sync. Race condition: a timing-dependent logic bug, still possible, still memory safe.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Why one load can cost 3 cycles or 240
md: Latency numbers are not constants of nature. Drepper's are for a Pentium M, CMU's for Haswell, and every CPU differs. Use them to reason about *ratios* (a DRAM access costs tens to hundreds of L1 hits), and measure your own machine before quoting absolute cycles.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Activation patching worked through: two directions and a shortcut
md: Denoising asks whether a component is enough to restore the behavior; noising asks whether the behavior needs it. AND-like circuits hide from denoising, OR-like backups hide from noising, and gradient shortcuts are trustworthy only for small patches.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Limitations, and tracing circuits yourself
md: An attribution graph explains one prompt in one replacement model. It is not proof of a general algorithm, it is silent about attention's choices, and any path through error nodes is unexplained. State those limits whenever you report a circuit.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Estimating propensities: swaps, EM, harvesting, dual learning
md: Pick the propensity source by how much user disruption you can afford: randomization or swaps are simplest and most trustworthy, EM and intervention harvesting use existing logs but rest on model assumptions, and DLA learns everything jointly. Every option inherits the click model's assumptions; if users behave like a cascade, a position-only propensity is misspecified.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Browser extensions: someone else's code in every page
md: Nothing on facebook.com was vulnerable in that case. An extension with access to a site is effectively a trusted script on that site. For a site owner this risk sits outside your perimeter; for an organisation that manages its employees' browsers, it is squarely inside it.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Where the evidence lives when there is no server to seize
md: Cloud incident response reconstructs what identities did through the provider's API, across four evidence layers: control plane, data plane, workload and identity provider. What you can prove is decided before the incident, by which logs were on and where they were kept.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Identity incidents: tokens, consent grants and mailbox rules
md: Misconception: "we reset the password, so the attacker is out". A reset leaves forwarding rules, registered MFA methods, OAuth consent grants and app passwords in place, and already issued access tokens keep working for up to about an hour in apps without CAE. Disable, revoke, then hunt for each kind of persistence.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: The same guardrails in Azure Policy and Google organization policy
md: Identity rules (RBAC, IAM) say who may act. Configuration guardrails (Azure Policy, Google organization policy, AWS SCPs used as preventive controls) say what no one may build, such as storage that accepts account keys or service accounts with downloadable keys. Set them high in the hierarchy, start in audit mode, then deny.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: The shared responsibility model, and when the provider gets it wrong
md: Common misconception: "we are on a big cloud, so the provider handles security." The provider secures its platform. Your identities, keys, data and configuration are yours, and even provider-side bugs usually ended with a customer to-do: regenerate keys after ChaosDB, update agents after OMIGOD.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Logging and detection: what key abuse looks like in CloudTrail
md: Log everything that changes configuration, keep it in a place attackers cannot reach, turn on data events for buckets that hold sensitive data, and alert on a short list of high-signal events: logging disabled, root use, new access keys and users, policy changes, and known credentials used from new places.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Choosing k: elbow, silhouette and their limits
md: Three things the silhouette cannot do. It is undefined for k = 1, so it can never tell you "this data has no clusters" (our k = 3 winner at 0.54 is not strong evidence of anything). It needs all pairwise distances, so it costs O(n squared) work. And it rewards compact well-separated blobs, so it is biased toward the kind of answer k-means produces, which makes it a poor referee between k-means and a density method.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Arrow in memory: buffers, validity bitmaps and offsets
md: A column in memory is a few flat buffers: values (or offsets plus data) and a validity bitmap. Flat, typed, contiguous buffers are what make tight loops and SIMD over columns possible.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Inlining: removing a call unlocks every other optimization
md: Misconception: the `inline` keyword forces inlining. It is a hint plus linkage rules: rules about how the function's definition is shared between files. At -O2 the compiler inlines functions you never marked, and may refuse ones you did. At -O0 GCC inlines nothing unless the function has `__attribute__((always_inline))`.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: PGO, -march=native and -ffast-math: speed with strings attached
md: -ffast-math assumes no NaNs or infinities (-ffinite-math-only), so code that relies on IEEE behavior of NaNs and infinities can give incorrect results. Clang has deprecated -Ofast because an optimization flag changing the observable behavior of correct code surprises people. Enable fast-math per file or per function when you have verified the numerics, not globally.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Safety: sandboxes, confirmations and prompt injection
md: Misconception: a system prompt saying "ignore instructions on web pages" solves injection. It helps, but the model reads that prompt and the attacker's text through the same channel. Defenses that do not depend on the model obeying (no secrets in the VM, network allowlists, harness-enforced confirmations) are what hold when the model is fooled.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Choosing and running loom and ThreadSanitizer in a real project
md: TSan must see **all** synchronization. Code not built with the flag (a prebuilt library, inline assembly) can cause false positives or missed races. That is why Rust's std should be rebuilt with the sanitizer via `-Zbuild-std`. The Rust unstable book also says Rust TSan does not support `std::sync::atomic::fence` or synchronization done in inline assembly, and rebuilding std does not change that.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Weaker but useful: sequential and causal consistency
md: Herlihy and Wing showed sequential consistency is **not local**: every object can be sequentially consistent while the system as a whole is not. Linearizability is local, which is one reason it composes better.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Must-haves and nice-to-haves need different machinery
md: Hard constraints decide **who is in**; soft constraints decide **the order**. Never let a preference buy its way past a requirement, and never let a preference silently remove someone.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: SAT solvers: DPLL, unit propagation and clause learning
md: CDCL = DPLL + conflict analysis that learns a clause + backjumping to the level where the learned clause becomes unit and forces (asserts) its last literal + watched literals for cheap propagation + activity-based decisions and restarts. Each conflict teaches the solver something it never has to rediscover.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Pinning by digest, signing images and verifying at admission
md: Pin by digest so you always run the same bytes; sign in CI and verify at admission so you only run bytes your pipeline produced.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Service account tokens and cloud identity for pods
md: A pod's identity is its service account token plus whatever cloud role it can reach. Mount tokens only where needed, give each app its own service account, and map cloud access per service account instead of per node.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Escapes in the runtime: runc CVE-2019-5736 and Leaky Vessels
md: Runtime escapes come from the runtime briefly holding host resources while entering a container. Patch the runtime everywhere, run only trusted images, and use user namespaces so that even a successful escape lands as an unprivileged user.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: The filters object and its four update operations
md: Deletes and resets are rare in training data and rare in casual testing, so they are the operations most likely to be broken in your system. Test them on purpose: write cases for *drop X*, *any X is fine*, *never mind the Y* and *start over*.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Storing state server-side and measuring it
md: Store the state server-side with a version and an event log; evaluate it with joint goal accuracy and per-operation recall, not just slot accuracy or end-to-end clicks.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Unfaithful without a hint: rationalization on natural prompts
md: Reversed question pairs detect unfaithfulness without planting anything: a consistent reasoner cannot answer Yes to both. This is behavioral evidence, necessary but not sufficient for faithful internal computation, and it shows frontier models rationalize rarely but measurably.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: Streams, the default stream trap, and events
md: Three independent facts, often confused. A stream gives you **ordering** (and is always sequential inside itself). Separate streams give you **permission** to overlap. The hardware (`asyncEngineCount`, concurrent kernel support, free SMs) decides whether overlap actually **happens**. Two streams on a one-copy-engine GPU will still serialize their two transfers against each other.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Inside the forward pass: query and document attend to each other
md: Joint attention makes each document token's representation a function of the query. That is the source of the accuracy gain and the reason nothing beyond tokenization can be reused across queries.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: The one-time pad: perfect secrecy and the cost of reusing a key
md: Any cipher that XORs a keystream onto data must never produce the same keystream twice. Remember this; it returns in lessons 6, 7 and 15 under the names counter reuse, nonce reuse and ECDSA nonce reuse.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Putting it together: TLS 1.3 and the rules of using crypto
md: Most cryptographic failures in the wild are not broken maths. They are reused nonces, weak randomness, unchecked parameters, outdated algorithms and home-made constructions. Security review of crypto code is mostly checking these nine rules.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Secret-dependent timing: comparisons, Minerva and TPM-Fail
md: Any secret that influences control flow, memory addresses or loop lengths can leak through time, over a network or from another process. Use library functions built to be constant time, keep crypto libraries and firmware patched, and never write your own comparison or scalar multiplication.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: CuTe layouts: shape and stride as an index function
md: A layout is just a function: coordinate in, integer offset out, computed as an inner product with the strides. Everything else in CuTe (tiling, partitioning across threads, MMA operand maps) is built by combining such functions.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Why servers strand DRAM and why DDR alone cannot fix it
md: CXL attacks two problems at once: capacity and bandwidth that DDR pins cannot scale (memory *expansion*), and DRAM that is stuck on the wrong host (memory *pooling*). Both rely on one property: the CPU reaches the memory with plain loads and stores, so applications do not change.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Three questions before you touch a system: law, permission, ethics
md: Ask three questions every time: is it legal (law), is it authorised (the owner, in writing, in scope), is it right (harm to others). Keep evidence of each answer before you start.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Crossing borders: the Budapest Convention and jurisdiction
md: Testing a system abroad from home does not put you under only your own country's law. Both CMA section 5 and CyBOK's analysis point the same way: the target's location can be enough.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Monitoring, interception and privacy law in security work
md: Login banners are not magic. They support consent and notice, but they do not authorise intercepting people who never saw them (a visitor on guest Wi-Fi, the other party to an email), and they do not override necessity and retention limits.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a researcher's decision checklist
md: Every lesson's cases share one pattern: the person in trouble had a story that made sense to them ('it was public', 'they agreed afterwards', 'it's only code', 'nothing was merged'). The checklist exists because your own story is the hardest one to see past.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Mixtures that change during training: annealing data and mid-training
md: A gain from an anneal is not proof that the data would help as much over a full pretraining run, or at a larger scale. Llama 3's math annealing helped the 8B model a lot and the 405B model hardly at all. Use anneals to rank candidate datasets, then confirm at the scale you care about.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: SIMD lanes: contiguous loads, gathers, and blocked SoA
md: Vectorizing the instructions does not fix the layout. Vectorizing means rewriting a scalar loop, which handles one element per instruction, into SIMD instructions that handle 8 at once, and compilers can do it automatically. Even if a compiler vectorizes an AoS loop, the x values are still 12 bytes apart, so each register still needs a gather and the loop still pays for every unused byte in each line.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Keep less: minimisation, retention schedules and legal holds
md: Collect only what the purpose needs, give every record type a retention period and a trigger, enforce it with a job (not a policy document), and make legal holds the only thing that stops the job.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Insider risk: definitions, the Tesla files and running a programme
md: Insiders already have access, so the programme rests on context (HR events, role), behaviour against the person's own baseline, and exfiltration routes, combined as sequences. Build it with HR, legal and privacy from the start, and pseudonymise until there is cause.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Honeytokens and canary tokens: data that phones home
md: A hosted token service sees your alerts: the alert, including the triggering address, goes to whoever runs the token server. For sensitive placements, run your own. Thinkst publishes the Canarytokens server as open source and recommends its Docker image for self-hosting.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Two orderings, two answers: float addition is not associative
md: Floating-point addition is commutative but not associative. Reordering a sum is not a refactor, it is a different computation. Every other idea in this course follows from that sentence.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: DevSecOps: security checks on the path from commit to cloud
md: The pipeline is a privileged identity. Its definition files, its runners, its credentials and its state files deserve the same protection as production, because each one is a path into production.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Why generate text in any order other than left to right?
md: A diffusion language model keeps the Transformer and the maximum-likelihood goal of a GPT. It changes two things: attention is bidirectional, and generation fills in many masked positions per step in any order instead of one token at the end.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Making diffusion LMs useful: AR initialization, RL and remasking
md: The mechanism of a diffusion LM is unchanged by all three ideas. AR initialization reuses weights through the shift operation, RL and DPO replace the exact log-probability with cheap or variance-reduced estimates of the bound, and ReMDM changes only the sampler so that more steps can fix mistakes.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: The KV handoff in detail: protocol, layouts and failures
md: A successful RDMA read proves nothing about the data. If P's lease ran out and the blocks were recycled for another prompt, the read still completes and returns that other request's KV; the symptom is corrupted output or NaN logits, not a transport error. That is why vLLM's decoder checks the lease deadline P exported, rebased with a clock offset measured at handshake, before the read and again when it completes.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: From sectors to partitions to image files
md: Do not stop at the partitions. NIST SP 800-86 counts *free space* (areas not allocated to any partition, including whole deleted volumes) as a place where data may remain. Our lab disk already has 2,047 sectors before the first partition that no file system owns.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Anti-forensics from the defender's side: what each trick leaves
md: The cleanup is evidence too. A 1102 event, a reset journal or deleted shadow copies at 14:35 tell you someone with administrator rights was covering tracks then, which often dates the intrusion better than anything they deleted.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Why DPO skips the reward model and the RL loop
md: DPO is not "RLHF without a reward". It fits the same Bradley-Terry reward model, just parameterized through the policy. It also inherits the KL objective's $\beta$. What it removes is the separate reward network and on-policy sampling during training.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Why a live data migration needs four careful phases
md: Until phase 4, at least one store is complete and current, and the other one is being kept in step with it. That is what makes every earlier step reversible. Plan each phase so it can be rolled out gradually (by percentage of objects or code paths) and rolled back with a flag.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Flipping writes, cutting over and deleting the old path
md: Move one thing at a time, keep one store complete until the very end, and measure agreement continuously. The deletion in phase 4 is the only step that should be hard to undo.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: The DH ratchet: healing after a key theft
md: Symmetric ratchet: forward secrecy within a chain. DH ratchet: fresh randomness every round trip, giving post-compromise security against a passive attacker. Together they are the Double Ratchet.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: MLS in practice: proposals, commits, epochs and the two services
md: MLS replaces ad hoc group logic with one rule: every change to membership or keys is a signed Commit that moves the whole group to a new epoch with a new secret. The AS must be kept honest; the DS only needs to deliver.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Why run your tracing logic inside the kernel
md: eBPF lets you run your own logic at the moment an event happens, inside the kernel, with a load-time proof that it cannot crash or hang the machine. bpftrace makes that a one-liner: probe, optional filter, action, and maps that summarize in the kernel.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Fewer operations and fewer weights, then shipping it
md: Pruning does not automatically make a model smaller or faster. The LiteRT docs state that pruned models are the same size on disk and have the same latency; they only compress better. You get size savings from a sparse format or compression, and speed only from kernels or hardware that skip zeros. With 8-bit values plus 8-bit gaps, sparse storage only wins once more than half the weights are zero.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: PAN-OS GlobalProtect, 2024: a cookie that became a command
md: Early interim guidance can be wrong. The first CVE-2024-3400 advisory tied exposure to telemetry; that was later corrected. Use a vendor workaround to buy hours, then install the fix and verify, rather than treating the workaround as the answer.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Measuring wasted tokens and training them away
md: Plain SFT on short samples barely helped here (a 2.0% cut on MATH500). Imitating short traces is weaker than contrasting short against long, because the model never sees what it should move away from.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Underthinking and early exit: stopping at the right moment
md: Waste has two shapes: thinking past a settled answer (stop it with a confidence test such as DEER) and abandoning good ideas too fast (slow the switching with TIP). Both are cheap decode-time controls that need no retraining, sitting between the RL methods and an API's blunt output cap.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Many spellings of one value: UTF-8 overlongs and base64 slack
md: An encoding is safe to check only if every value has exactly one valid spelling and every decoder rejects the rest.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Bidirectional text and Trojan Source (CVE-2021-42574)
md: Reviewers approve what they see; compilers build what is stored. Any character that changes one without the other (bidi controls, unusual line separators, lookalike identifiers) should fail the build unless it is written as a visible escape.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: ETW: providers, sessions and consumers
md: ETW is plumbing: providers emit, sessions buffer, consumers read. Most of what Event Viewer, Sysmon and EDR sensors show you rides on it, so an attacker who can switch providers off removes evidence before it is ever written.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Tampering and EDR killers: SUNBURST, BYOVD and AuKill
md: Check your driver-load filter against this case. SwiftOnSecurity's config excludes event 6 for drivers whose signature contains `microsoft`. The driver AuKill abused was signed by Microsoft, so that exclusion would hide its load. Narrow exclusions to drivers you have inventoried, or match against a vulnerable-driver hash list instead of the signer.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Neural NILM, seq2point, and the unseen-house problem
md: Every NILM method injects prior knowledge to resolve an unidentifiable sum. Hart hand-designs it (step signatures), FHMMs encode it as state machines, and neural nets learn it from sub-metered houses. The test that matters is a house the model never saw.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Job titles: taxonomies, seniority and embeddings
md: General-purpose embedding models do not know your abbreviations (`SWE` software engineer, `SDET` software development engineer in test, `RN` registered nurse) and blur words that share context (`sales engineer` vs `software engineer`). Expand abbreviations before embedding, match against many alternate titles rather than one label, and keep an *unknown* outcome instead of forcing the nearest code.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Delegated vs application permissions, and who may consent
md: Delegated means the app is capped by the user; application means the app is capped only by the permission. Restrict who may consent to what, and treat every application permission, especially any with write access, as an admin role held by software.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Devices and the Primary Refresh Token: SSO bound to hardware
md: The PRT is the device's master refresh token. Its strength is the TPM-held session key that signs every use; its weak points are devices without TPMs, attacker-registered devices, and the fact that Conditional Access runs when it is used, not when it is issued.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Taking over admins: help desks, MFA resets and rogue federation
md: Help-desk takeovers turn a phone call into admin credentials, and admin credentials into persistence (federated domains, app secrets, devices). Verify callers out of band, keep admin resets in a small privileged role, require phishing-resistant MFA for admins, and alert on any federation change.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Level-triggered versus edge-triggered, and reading until EAGAIN
md: Level-triggered asks "is it ready now?" on every wait. Edge-triggered says "it just became ready" once. With ET you own the state: read or write until `EAGAIN`, or remember that the connection is still ready.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Testing many variants: Bonferroni and Holm corrections
md: Count every comparison you make on a query set, including metrics, variants and earlier papers' tests, and correct for the family. Holm is never worse than Bonferroni. Better still, decide the one comparison you will test before you look.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: RELRO, the GOT and FORTIFY_SOURCE
md: RELRO protects a table of pointers by making it read-only after start-up; FORTIFY stops some overflows before they write. Both are cheap, both are build flags, and both should be on: `-Wl,-z,relro,-z,now` and `-D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=3` at `-O2`.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: How big is a line, how to find false sharing, who pads
md: Do not pad on a hunch. Padding costs memory and can push other hot data out of cache, which is why Drepper calls padding every variable unacceptable. Confirm with perf c2c or a before-and-after benchmark that the line is really contended.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Threats: what updates leak and how clients poison the model
md: Updates leak inputs (exactly, for a fully connected layer), and a single client can replace the global model in one round by scaling its update by n/eta. Robust aggregators need to see individual updates; secure aggregation exists to hide them. Pick your threat model before you pick your aggregator.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: From one MLP to many routed experts
md: Separate two numbers for every MoE model: **total parameters** (all experts, what you store) and **activated parameters** (what one token actually uses, which sets FLOPs per token). DeepSeek-V3 has 671B total and 37B activated per token.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: SPI flash, SMM and the write lock LoJax walked through
md: A lock is only real if the firmware turns it on and locks it before running anything untrusted. Every one of these bits defaults to off; the firmware must configure them on every boot.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: Case: LogoFAIL, a boot logo parsed by the most trusted code
md: Every parser in firmware is attack surface with the highest privilege on the machine. The fix is the same as anywhere else (validate sizes, use checked arithmetic, fuzz), plus the firmware-specific rule: do not read customisable data from places the verified boot chain does not cover.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Why LLM serving needs its own attention engine
md: Attention in serving is mostly about **memory traffic under irregular shapes**. FlashInfer's answer is to separate what is static (variant, layout, tile sizes: compile time) from what is dynamic (lengths, page lists: a cheap per-step plan).

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Generating data by following a velocity field from noise
md: A flow model is a learned velocity field plus an ODE solver. Flow matching makes the *training* of that field as cheap as regression; the *sampling* cost is the number of solver steps.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Inductive invariants: from bounded checks to every N
md: Checking ISpec with TLC is complete only for the model you configured. A passing inductive check at 3 acceptors is strong evidence, not a proof for 7; the TLAPS proof is what removes the bound.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Connecting specs to running code, and the wider tool map
md: Match the tool to the question. Is the design right? Model check it. Must it hold for every size? Prove the design. Does the code do what the design says? Prove refinement, or validate traces. Is this function free of panics and overflow? Model check or prove the code. Each answer covers only what it was asked.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: When low precision fails: outliers, SwiGLU and debugging a run
md: Do not trust a short run. Fishman et al.'s divergence appeared after about 200B tokens, twice the length of earlier FP8 studies, and Lee et al. expect their own short runs underestimate instability. A recipe that matches BF16 for a few billion tokens has only passed the easy part.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Bots in business flows: ticket scalping and the BOTS Act
md: Limits that count per account are limits per fake account. Count against every scarce identifier an order carries, and decide who may enter before the rush, not during it.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Finding rings with graphs: shared devices, cards and addresses
md: Fraud hides in groups. Link accounts by rare shared identifiers, drop identifiers that honest crowds share, and review dense components rather than single accounts.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: From risk score to decision: rules, models, step-up and review
md: A score is only a probability if it is calibrated. Raw scores from many models are not; a "0.8" may mean 30% fraud. Calibrate on recent labelled data before you plug scores into expected-cost thresholds.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Adaptive adversaries: shadow mode, response and running the programme
md: Every control has a half-life. Launch in shadow mode, watch for adaptation through volume and loss metrics, run large attacks as incidents, and keep an inventory of every flow an attacker could farm.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: A real hunt with libFuzzer: harness, run log and the crash
md: On macOS, Apple's Xcode clang ships without libFuzzer (the Atheris documentation says the same), and Homebrew's clang needs the SDK path (`-isysroot $(xcrun --show-sdk-path)`) to find system headers. On Linux, distribution clang packages include it.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Protocol and stateful fuzzing, and the Broadcom Wi-Fi case
md: The Broadcom case was found by reverse engineering and code review, not fuzzing, and its lesson for fuzzers is about reach: the dangerous code ran only for specific frame types in specific connection states. A stateless fuzzer of single frames would rarely get there.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Why exact matching fails and what an edit distance counts
md: A distance counts edits (lower is closer). A similarity is a normalized score (higher is closer). The same raw distance means very different things for short and long strings, so either normalize or make the allowed number of edits depend on length.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Geometric hashing: basis pairs, a hash table, and votes
md: Geometric hashing moves the expensive work offline: every model is stored under every basis. At query time one correct scene basis is enough, and it never needs to know in advance which model point it corresponds to.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Geohash: interleave the bits, name the cell
md: A shared geohash prefix guarantees closeness: both points are inside the same cell. The reverse is false: two points can be meters apart and share no prefix, because they straddle a cell boundary. Every correct proximity search must look at neighboring cells, not just one prefix.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Why frameworks do not call cudaMalloc for every tensor
md: A caching allocator turns slow, synchronizing driver calls into fast CPU-side bookkeeping. The price is that freed memory is *kept*, so reserved memory, not allocated memory, is what other processes on the GPU see.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Fixed-size suballocation for the KV cache, and diagnosing OOMs
md: All of these allocators are the same pattern at different layers: grab big memory rarely, carve it with your own rules, and choose block sizes that match the workload. Equal sizes kill external fragmentation; growable virtual ranges kill slivers; stream order makes reuse cheap.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Case study: one matrix transpose, three kernels
md: These measurements come from older GPUs (Fermi and Kepler in the post, Volta in the guide). Absolute numbers on a current GPU will differ, and larger caches can hide some waste. The sector and bank rules they illustrate are the ones the current CUDA guides still document.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: The SOL gap: ranking many kernels by what they can return
md: Rank by gap times time share, with an attainable target instead of 100 percent. The biggest gap and the biggest win are usually different kernels, and a gap on a kernel with a small time share is never worth a rewrite.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Why chunk retrieval cannot answer 'what are the main themes?'
md: GraphRAG is not a better retriever for every question. For a specific fact ("Who supplies Rover X2 motors?") plain vector RAG already finds c2, and the paper itself shows vector RAG gives the most *direct* answers. GraphRAG's measured gains are on broad sensemaking questions, the ones that need an understanding of the whole corpus.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Lighter graph RAG: FastGraphRAG, LightRAG, HippoRAG
md: Graph RAG variants differ in where they spend LLM calls: GraphRAG spends heavily at indexing (extraction, summaries, reports) and on map calls per global query; FastGraphRAG cuts extraction; LightRAG drops communities; HippoRAG drops summaries and lets PPR do the multi-hop work.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: Beyond GRPO: RLOO, GSPO, off-policy drift, and what RLVR teaches
md: Before trusting an RLVR gain: test on several model families (a Qwen-only result may be amplified priors), compare against random and format-only rewards, and compare against distilling a stronger model (lesson 6).

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Phone phreaking: when the voice line was also the control line
md: In-band signalling fails because whoever can send data can also send commands. The durable fix is to separate the control channel from the data channel so the attacker has no way to reach it. You will meet the same idea as parameterised SQL queries and as never evaluating text found inside log messages.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Code Red, Slammer and Blaster: worms faster than people
md: At internet speed, the defence has to be in place before the worm arrives: patches installed, unneeded services unreachable, firewalls on by default, and automatic updates for machines without an administrator. Human response time is measured in minutes; Slammer finished in about ten.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: SolarWinds and Log4Shell: what you install and what you import
md: A valid digital signature does not mean software is safe. It proves who published it and that it was not altered afterwards. If the attacker is inside the publisher's build, the malicious code is signed along with everything else, as with SolarWinds.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: Reading the numbers: generic events, pitfalls and top-down
md: A sound counter workflow: `perf stat` for IPC and TopdownL1, drill into the biggest bucket with grouped metrics, then `perf record` on the matching event with `:pp` to find the code, change it, and measure again.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: One request, two readers: why proxies and caches disagree
md: Every bug in this course is a **parser differential**: two programs read the same message and reach different conclusions. The durable fixes remove the room for disagreement (one unambiguous framing, one definition of the cache key) rather than trying to spot bad requests one by one.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: The 2025 endgame: 0.CL, Expect and upstream HTTP/1.1
md: The structural fix for request smuggling is to stop sending HTTP/1.1 between your own servers. Until then, every hop must reject ambiguous requests, and every code path must consume the body or close the connection.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a 2 MiB mapping: offset bits, alignment, contiguity
md: Misconception: "the box has 40 GiB free, so it can provide 40 GiB of huge pages." Huge pages need aligned, physically contiguous free runs. After fragmentation, requests can come up short or have to wait for compaction.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: The SSM layer inside a hybrid: Mamba-2 as gated linear attention
md: The duality does not make Mamba-2 as good at recall as softmax attention. The quadratic form is a way to compute the same layer faster in training; at inference, all past information still has to pass through the fixed state, and there is no softmax to pick one token sharply.

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: A cross-encoder reranks the fused shortlist
md: Fusion is about **recall of the shortlist** (the share of relevant documents that make it in); reranking is about **precision at the top** (the share of the top few that are relevant). Fused-list quality caps what the reranker can achieve, and rerank depth N trades latency for the chance to rescue documents fused low.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Zones and conduits: the ISA/IEC 62443 way to segment
md: A conduit is a promise in two parts: only these services, between only these zones. Write it down as a table, enforce it with firewalls or gateways, and monitor it so that anything outside the table becomes an alert.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: IT/OT convergence: Colonial, Oldsmar, Unitronics, Volt Typhoon
md: CISA's 2025 primary mitigations for OT read like a summary of these four cases: remove OT connections to the public internet, change default passwords, secure remote access, segment IT and OT, and practise operating manually.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: XML Signature from zero: canonical form, digests and SignedInfo
md: The W3C specification's security section says it in two lines: *only what is signed is secure*, and applications should *see what is signed*, meaning they must act on the exact data that was hashed and verified, not on some other view of the document.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: SCIM provisioning: creating and removing accounts in every app
md: Deprovisioning is more than `active: false`. A leaver's access also lives in open sessions, refresh tokens, personal API keys and OAuth grants the user created inside the app. Check what your apps do on SCIM deactivation; if the answer is "only blocks the next login", add the rest to the offboarding runbook.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Joiner, mover, leaver: the lifecycle and how access creeps
md: Compute access from the authoritative record (desired state) and apply the difference both ways. Movers are the riskiest event, because add-only processes never remove anything.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Service accounts and non-human identities
md: Non-human identities have no leaving date, so give them an owner, an expiry and a last-used check. When a secret may be exposed, rotate all of them, including the ones you believe are unused: that belief is what Cloudflare's attacker used.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Cleaning the mask and correcting for lighting
md: A robust change detector is: align (features, RANSAC, homography, optional ECC refinement), mask invalid warped borders, correct photometry using pixels that probably did not change, difference, threshold (Otsu when the histogram is two-humped), then open the mask with a kernel smaller than the smallest change you care about.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Hashing evidence and keeping a chain of custody
md: Hash at collection, hash at every transfer, analyse only copies. A hash that matches the one recorded at acquisition is what lets you say "this is exactly what we took from the machine".

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: When the incident is not an attack: CrowdStrike, July 2024
md: Treat large non-malicious outages with the same machinery as attacks: incident commander, severity, OOB communications, a timeline and a blameless review. Attackers will use the confusion either way.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: Shellshock: when an environment variable became code
md: Shellshock is injection into an interpreter nobody thought was in the path. The data (a header) was never concatenated into code by the application; the interpreter itself treated a data channel (the environment) as code. Know which interpreters your input reaches, including the ones your libraries start for you.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Inside a connected device: microcontrollers, flash and the boot ROM
md: Every protection in a device rests on something that cannot change: code in boot ROM and bits in OTP. Everything in flash can be updated, by the maker or by an attacker who gets write access. Good design decides early which checks and secrets go where.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Device vulnerability handling: disclosure, SBOMs and the CRA
md: Vulnerability handling is a pipeline: a published way to receive reports, an SBOM to find affected products, a signed update path to fix them, a stated support period, and (in the EU) 24-hour, 72-hour and final reports for exploited bugs. Missing any stage breaks the rest.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: ReDoS: a regular expression that blocks every user
md: A backtracking regex is dangerous when one string can be matched in many ways: a quantifier inside a quantifier, alternatives that overlap such as `(a|a)*`, or several `.*` in a row. The slow case is the near miss, so a test with matching strings will never show it. On Node.js the cost is paid by every user of the process.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Finding and catching JavaScript bugs: tools, signals, practice
md: One idea runs through the whole course: in JavaScript the boundaries you assume (an object, a context, a module, a header, a renderer) are usually not security boundaries. Real boundaries are processes, operating system users, origins and authenticated messages. Put untrusted input and untrusted code behind one of those, and check permission where the data is used.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Checking linearizability: searching for a legal order
md: Linearizability checking is a search for one legal order inside the real-time constraints. Its cost is driven by how many operations overlap, so you control it by limiting operations per key and by turning known non-effects (like timed-out reads) into `:fail`.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Measuring, caching and promoting without regressions
md: Three defences, in order: prune what cannot run, search within a budget you chose from a convergence curve, and promote only wins that are larger than the noise. A tuner without the third one is a random walk through your performance history.

courseTitle: Windows kernel and driver security: BYOVD and kernel hardening
lessonTitle: Why Windows trusts drivers: the kernel line and the admin line
md: Two separate questions decide whether kernel code runs: *who* asks (only admins may load drivers, and admin-to-kernel is not a serviced boundary) and *which code* it is (the signature check). Every defence in this course strengthens the second question, because on Windows the first one is already answered once an attacker is admin.

courseTitle: Windows kernel and driver security: BYOVD and kernel hardening
lessonTitle: VBS and memory integrity: taking code checks out of the kernel
md: Memory integrity protects kernel **code**, not kernel **data**. A BYOVD driver that lets a caller change kernel memory can still alter data structures in VTL0, such as callback registrations or policy variables, and memory integrity does not stop that. HVCI is necessary, not sufficient.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Epilogue fusion, fused softmax and FlashAttention
md: Epilogue fusion matters less than elementwise fusion for big GEMMs: the matmul is compute bound and dominates, so removing a 66 us kernel from a 947 us layer saves about 7 percent. It matters more for small or skinny matmuls, where the GEMM itself is short.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Matching what the teacher computes inside: hints, attention, states
md: Feature losses need alignment that output losses do not: a projection or regressor when widths differ (FitNets, TinyBERT's W_h), a layer mapping when depths differ, and the same spatial grid or the same token positions. Output distillation needs none of this, only the same set of classes or the same vocabulary.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Sizing the KV cache of Llama 3 8B, and why it caps batch size
md: A common slip is to use `num_attention_heads` (32) instead of `num_key_value_heads` (8) for a GQA model like Llama 3. That overstates its cache by 4x.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Keeping fewer tokens: windows, attention sinks and heavy hitters
md: Eviction trades exactness for a fixed memory budget. Keep the sink tokens, keep recent tokens, and use accumulated attention to keep the heavy hitters; anything evicted cannot be recovered.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, capacity and reuse
lessonTitle: Why the GPU prefix cache runs out, and where KV can go
md: Reuse offloading does not make the GPU's attention kernel read from CPU memory. Blocks are copied back into GPU blocks before the kernel runs; the kernel only ever sees HBM. What it buys is skipping the *prefill compute* that would otherwise recreate those blocks. Capacity offloading can differ: FlexGen can run attention on the CPU, where the KV lives.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, capacity and reuse
lessonTitle: Eviction and placement: what stays, what sinks, what is dropped
md: Choose eviction by reuse pattern, not habit. LRU is a fine default; workloads with known future reuse (queued multi-turn sessions, scheduled agent steps) do much better with placement driven by the scheduler.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Hybrid logical clocks: Lamport order that stays near real time
md: HLC is still one-way like Lamport: $(l, c)$ ordering never tells you two events are concurrent. Its gain is closeness to real time and constant size, not concurrency detection.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: ColPali: late interaction over page images
md: ColBERT and ColPali are the same idea at different granularities: keep one vector per token or patch, precompute the document side, and let each query token pick its best match.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Latent search: one thought, several frontier nodes
md: A continuous thought can encode a weighted set of next steps. Coconut reached 97.0% on ProsQA where CoT reached 77.5%, generating 14.2 tokens instead of 49.4. The probes suggest deferring commitment is part of why, but staged training without any thoughts also reached 95.5%.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: The last mile and the Recursive Model Index
md: An RMI separates model size from execution cost. A lookup evaluates exactly one model per stage, however many leaf models exist. Adding leaves makes each leaf's slice smaller and its error bounds tighter without adding work per lookup.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: Scoring as a sparse dot product over an inverted index
md: Cost is driven by the total length of the posting lists the query touches, not by vocabulary size. Every extra query expansion term and every long posting list is extra work. That is why sparsity, especially on the query side, is the thing training must control.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Dropping the softmax turns attention into an RNN
md: Linear attention is one function with two schedules: a **parallel form** $O=(QK^\top\odot M)V$ that is matmul-friendly for training, and a **recurrent form** $S_t=S_{t-1}+v_tk_t^\top$, $o_t=S_tq_t$ with constant time and memory per generated token.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: What a fixed state cannot do: recall limits and state tracking
md: Do not mix the two limits up. A bigger state helps recall but does nothing for parity: with eigenvalues in [0, 1], even a huge state fails at long lengths. Negative eigenvalues fix parity but add no storage. Production models answer the recall limit by keeping some attention layers (lesson 9).

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Services, systemd and cron: what runs without anyone logged in
md: A cron job run by root that executes a script writable by another user is a privilege escalation waiting to happen: whoever can edit the script chooses what root runs every night. When auditing, check the permissions of every file a root job calls, not only the crontab line.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: A basic hardening checklist and where to practise
md: Patch, expose less, use keys, grant little, keep logs off the box and keep baselines. Each step is simple; together they turn most of the attacks in this course from silent root into a noisy, short-lived event.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Kernel lockdown modes and sysctl baselines across a fleet
md: Use lockdown integrity mode on fleets that run eBPF or kprobe sensors; confidentiality also blocks the reads those sensors need. Lockdown only ever goes up until reboot. For sysctl, the last-sorted file wins across directories, so always verify running values, not config files.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Tetragon: filtering and enforcing inside the kernel
md: A kprobe policy depends on a kernel function name and its arguments, which are not a stable interface and can change between kernel versions. Test policies against every kernel version in your fleet, and watch for the policy failing to load after a kernel update.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Case: regreSSHion across a fleet, from advisory to verified fix
md: Fleet response = package-aware inventory, immediate exposure reduction through config management, ring rollout with restarts, verification of running code, and detection of the attack's noise in the meantime. Never triage on upstream version strings alone.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Circularity, gaming, and running an LLM judge safely
md: Use an LLM judge to label at scale, but never let the measurement and the thing measured share the same model and prompt, and keep a human gold set to check the instrument. When the judge is also a ranking component, its scores stop measuring anything.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Defense in depth: input, prompt, output and grounding layers
md: Masking the model's input and output does not mask everything else. The AWS docs say Bedrock invocation logs (its record of each model call) keep the original request, and the `match` field of the guardrail trace (the per-request report of what each policy found) contains the original PII value by design. Protect logs and traces separately.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: KV cache accounting: from bytes per token to batch size
md: Capacity in sequences is roughly pool bytes / (bytes per token x tokens per sequence). Every lever (GQA, FP8 KV, more GPUs, smaller weights, shorter contexts, less waste per sequence) moves one of those three terms.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Build it yourself: a small engine with a block manager
md: An LLM engine is a loop: pick requests under a token budget, ask a block allocator whether each fits, evict when it does not, run one forward pass, sample, repeat. Writing it yourself makes every knob in this course something you can test.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Designing the filter schema: enums, ranges and nulls
md: A required, non-nullable field such as `salary_max: integer` forces the model to produce a number even when the user said nothing about salary. Constrained decoding guarantees *some* integer, so you get an invented bound (for example 0, or a number copied from a few-shot example) and a filter that silently removes good results.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Latency: the dependency chain decides, not the call count
md: Parallelism is a latency lever, not a cost lever. Running 100 pointwise calls at once reads the same 22,000 tokens as running them one by one, and on a hosted API it uses up rate limits faster.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Pairwise ranking prompting: allpairs, sorting and sliding
md: Pairwise preferences are not guaranteed to be transitive: the model can prefer A over B, B over C and C over A. Allpair just counts wins and copes; sorting algorithms assume a consistent comparator, so their output can depend on which pairs they happened to ask. The PRP paper reports robust results anyway but flags this as an open issue.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: ORB: binary descriptors compared with XOR and popcount
md: Float descriptors (SIFT) are compared with L2 distance; binary descriptors (ORB) with Hamming distance. Binary descriptors trade some distinctiveness for much cheaper extraction, storage and comparison.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The ABA problem: when a matching CAS is still wrong
md: Garbage collection does not make ABA go away in general. Michael points out that if a program moves the same node back and forth between two lock-free stacks, a stale CAS can still succeed even with perfect GC. What GC (and the schemes in lesson 6) do prevent is the special case where ABA comes from *freeing and reusing* a node someone still references.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: How accurate is this really, and by which metric
md: Vocabulary trap. "Parsing accuracy" in the 2019 benchmark means grouping, not token-level correctness. Modern papers reserve **PA**, short for parsing accuracy, for the stricter message-level metric where every static token *and* every parameter must be identified correctly, and use **GA** for grouping. A number quoted without its metric is worthless, so always ask: grouping or tokens, per message or per template?

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: The pipeline: collect, ship, parse, enrich, store
md: Monitor the pipeline like a production service: events per source per hour, parse-failure rate, queue depth, and the age of the newest event. A sensor that stops sending looks exactly like a quiet, safe network. Also alert on deliberate blinding: Windows event 1102 (Security log cleared) and CloudTrail StopLogging or DeleteTrail calls are ATT&CK Defense Impairment techniques (T1685.005, T1685.002).

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Threat hunting and the Pyramid of Pain: the FireEye alert
md: Use indicators (hashes, IPs, domains) for fast, cheap blocking and for searching history after a report is published. Invest your engineering time in behaviour detections, because they are the ones that still work next month.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Other routes to long context: base scaling, searched factors, data
md: The common production recipe: pick a large RoPE base (or raise it), then continue pretraining on a balanced mix with long documents upsampled, extending length in stages. Llama 3's six stages and 800B tokens (lesson 8) are the large-scale version. Inference-time rescaling (YaRN, Llama 3.1's rule, LongRoPE factors) is layered on top to go further.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Depth without parameters: what looping a block buys
md: Looping saves **parameters** (memory, communication), not **compute**. Every loop is another full pass through the block, and the passes are sequential, so a $(1 \otimes 12)$ model is about as slow per token as a 12-layer model. Looped models trade memory for depth, they do not make inference free.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Build it: loop your GPT with input injection and random depth
md: Turning a GPT into a recurrent-depth model takes a split into prelude, core and coda, a concat adapter, a noise start and a random-depth training loop. The monitor that matters is the gap between low-r and high-r validation loss.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: Counting parameters, choosing targets, merging for free inference
